title: Formal Assumptions and Sample-Size Planning
paragraphs: Appendix E Formal Assumptions and Sample-Size Planning E.1 Anchored Reputation-Update Contraction For the update in Equation 3.3, assume a xed nonnegative row-stochastic matrix A, a xed input vector X, and 0 < λ < 1. Let F(B) = (1 −λ)AB + λX. Then ∥F(B) −F(C)∥∞≤(1 −λ)∥A∥∞∥B −C∥∞= (1 −λ)∥B −C∥∞. (E.1) Since 1 −λ < 1, this is a contraction on the nite-dimensional real vector space. Its unique xed point is B∗= λ[I −(1 −λ)A]−1X. (E.2) The inverse exists because the spectral radius of (1−λ)A is less than one. This result does not apply without modication to arbitrary signed weights or time-varying inputs. It also does not imply that the consensus is factually correct: accuracy depends on the inputs and the measurement process. 261

APPENDIX E. FORMAL ASSUMPTIONS AND SAMPLE-SIZE PLANNING 262 E.2 Scope of the Free-Energy Analogy Consider the explicitly separable objective F(W, p) = L(W) −TH(p), H(p) = − m X j=1 pj log pj, T > 0, (E.3) with p a probability vector. If there are no additional constraints and L is independent of p, minimizing the entropy term gives the uniform distribution pj = 1/m. Indeed, interior stationarity of T P j pj log pj+µ(P j pj−1) gives T(log pj+1)+µ = 0, so all components are equal; convexity supplies the minimum. Stationarity of L alone does not establish a global minimum in a nonconvex model. These observations do not prove that the platform's actual dynamics minimize this objective, that its xed points coincide with these stationary points, or that a signed interaction matrix has a universal stable gain 1/λmax. Such claims require a specied dynamical system and a separate stability argument. The Hamiltonian in EST is therefore retained as a modelling proposal, not as a proof of social thermodynamic laws. E.3 Planning Calculation and Actual Recruitment The supplied summary lists an assumed standardised eect of .40, two-sided α = .05, target power .80, a nominal requirement of 52, and a recruitment target of 60. The original derivation uses a paired or one-sample normal approximation: n ≈ z1−α/2 + z1−β d 2 = 1.960 + .842 .40 2 ≈49.1. (E.4)

APPENDIX E. FORMAL ASSUMPTIONS AND SAMPLE-SIZE PLANNING 263 Rounding this approximation upward gives 50, not 52. An exact test calculation requires a specied test and the denition of the standardised eect; the export's nominal 52 is preserved as a planning entry rather than derived from this approximation. To retain 52 participants after an anticipated 15% loss would require Ntarget = 52 .85 = 62. (E.5) The actual study collected 60 records and retained 52 after eight historical exclusions. The documented response-and-context lter now reproduces those exclusions; these counts are not changed by the planning correction. Neither a pairedtest planning formula nor the number of simulated agents establishes power for an independent-groups eld experiment, a multivariate factor model, or an unmeasured learning endpoint.
